youtube_title: Fish Lake, Indiana: the handcar, the fast freight and Swift's lost ice houses (1897)
youtube:
You asked for Fish Lake! In 1897, a Grand Trunk section boss, John Sent, was taking workers by handcar to Swift and Company's ice houses at Mill Creek, near Upper Fish Lake. A fast freight came out of the night. A Chesterton paper said the men jumped for their lives, and Sent was killed while trying to move his handcar. Swift, the Chicago meatpacker, had bought the land around both Fish Lakes in 1888 and 1889 and cut the lakes into ice each winter. A 1978 county history says lightning later struck two of Swift's three giant ice houses, and they burned. It says the ice cutting ended in 1930, Swift sold out in 1935, and the buildings came down. Comment your town, and it could be next! #FishLake #LaPorteCounty #Indiana #History #LaPorteAfterDark #Shorts

All pictures are drawn; no one is shown hurt. Narration is a computer voice. Sources: The Westchester Tribune (Chesterton), "Section Boss Killed by a Train," Oct. 16, 1897, via Porter County INGenWeb; The Portable LaPorte County (c.1978, Michigan City Public Library); Fern Eddy Schultz, LaPorte County Historian (2019); Margaret B. Barker, Newspaper-Real Estate Schemes of the 1920s (2021), via Wikipedia; Wikipedia, Mill Creek, Indiana. More LaPorte County history: https://laporteweathernow.com/history

factcheck: Blind independent check Nov. 16, 2026 (script, on-screen text and pictures only), then a second check of the changes: the 1897 paper says the ice houses were 'at Mill Creek', so the line says 'at Mill Creek, near Upper Fish Lake'; '1888' became '1888 and 1889'; 'two of Swift's three' ice houses; the buildings came down after the 1935 sale, not in 1930; the lightning picture shows one house burning and two standing; the ice harvest shows a crew. The handcar death rests on one paper and the lightning on the 1978 booklet, both credited in the narration. Second check: all supported. After the second check, beat 7 became one sentence under 'It says', because the 1935 sale and the tearing down rest on the booklet alone, and the crew and sled driver were redrawn in short coats over trousers (the flared coats read as dresses).
